modeling_assumptions.text: Which physicians the training program would cover, if recommended: this case takes the hospital group's own language ('provide training to its physicians') to mean all 1,852 physicians, not only the 1,228 primary care physicians the underlying study actually surveyed. A narrower reading is equally defensible and changes the total dollar cost (and therefore cost-as-percent-of-profit) substantially -- see sensitivity_model.py's trained_physician_count FLEX dial.

How many years of the given six-year profit history count as 'typical' when judging the training's affordability: this case averages all six years equally. Weighting only the most recent years (profit nearly doubled 2015->2016 and fell back 2017->2018) is an equally defensible reading and produces a different 'typical profit' denominator -- see sensitivity_model.py's profit_window_years FLEX dial.

How to treat the 13 of 122 physicians whose time estimate was never recorded: this case treats the 109 recorded responses as missing-at-random and analyzes them as the full working sample. The missingness is NOT evenly distributed across weight-condition groups (see the authored Twist, FACILITATOR.md) -- this is a real, disclosed limitation the case deliberately does not resolve for the student.

deliverables.text: Three histograms of the time spent with the physician, one each for the average-weight, overweight, and obese patient groups, with a written note on what each histogram's shape tells you about that group's data.
Three box-and-whisker plots, one per weight group, plotted on a shared scale, each correctly showing the minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum of that group's time data.
A percent-above-median table: what percentage of average-weight patients' visits ran longer than the overweight group's median time? Longer than the obese group's median time?

A mean-and-range comparison table breaking the time data down by patient gender (within each weight group) and by a patient age split, with a written judgment of whether gender, age, or weight status looks like the bigger factor.

An outlier check: identify any outlier(s) in the obese group's box plot, and explain how including or excluding it changes the mean vs. the median for that group, and which statistic you'd trust more.

appendices.title: Benedictus Hospital Group: Scale, Complaints, Finances, and the Training Option

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: How many of Benedictus's 1,852 physicians would actually enroll in and complete the training if the program were approved is a real-world forecast no amount of research today can resolve -- staffing turnover, department-by-department opt-in, and a phased rollout are all plausible and none is knowable in advance of the hospital group actually running the program. This is the same MA1 uncertainty already named in modeling_assumptions[]. Flexing it +/-50% swings the cost-as-percent-of-profit denominator enough that tier2_probes.py's relative-margin cap check registers a breach at both ends (295.4% at -50%, 31.8% at +50%), even though the case's own percentage-point framing (a 26.6% measured gap against a 6.7%-20.2% cost range) stays a defensible spread throughout and the winner (recommend the training) never flips.

Which of the six given profit years counts as the 'typical' year Ingrid should judge affordability against is a genuine forecast/judgment question, not a knowable fact -- profit nearly doubled 2015->2016 and fell back 2017->2018, so no single window is objectively correct, and the actually relevant figure (the hospital's real future-year profit when the training bill comes due) cannot be known in advance at all. This is the same MA2 uncertainty already named in modeling_assumptions[]. Flexing the window +/-50% swings the same cost-as-percent-of-profit denominator enough to breach tier2_probes.py's relative-margin cap check (190.7% at -50%, 97.7% at +50%, the latter clamped to the full 6-year history since only 6 years are given), though the winner never flips across any tested window.

balance.argument_a: Across the real dataset, average-weight patients' physicians expected to spend a mean of 31.4 minutes with them, versus 23.0 minutes for overweight-and-obese patients combined -- a real, disclosed 26.6% gap. That gap, in percentage terms, is bigger than the training program's own total cost measured against a typical year's profit (13.4% of the 6-year average, at the case's default reading of who gets trained) -- the size of the measured problem outweighs the size of the ask, and the per-physician cost ($265) is small next to the cost of a single serious discrimination complaint reaching a human-rights tribunal (Appendix E).
balance.argument_b: A half-million-dollar program ($490,780 at this case's own default 1,852-physician reading) is a real, meaningful expense for an operator averaging a 1.4% ten-year profit margin -- not a rounding error under any of the profit-averaging windows Appendix D considers. The underlying evidence is also one single-scenario experiment (a migraine visit) from one research study, with 13 of 122 physicians' responses missing and no confirmation the missingness is random -- and the missingness is NOT evenly spread across the weight groups (the authored Twist). Committing a hospital-wide mandate on an incomplete dataset from one visit type, before replicating the finding, is a defensible position too.
balance.margin_basis: The two percentages Ingrid weighs side by side: the measured time-spent gap (26.6%, Appendix B's real, cited dataset) vs. the training's total cost as a percent of a typical year's profit (13.4%, Appendix C's given data at this case's default assumptions). Margin = 26.6 - 13.4 = 13.1 percentage points -- close enough to genuinely debate, and directly the arithmetic Challenge D3/D4 walks the student through building the pieces of. See derived{} for the full worked figures; sensitivity_model.py confirms this margin stays under the SPEC.md Section 2 20% cap across every tested +/-50% flex of either stated modeling assumption.
balance.stability: WINNER-STABLE, DISCLOSED-NOT-ELIMINATED under a +/-50% flex of both stated modeling assumptions (see sensitivity_model.py, probe 5; case.json.sensitivity_disclosure[]). The winner never flips: Option A (recommend) leads at every tested flex of both dials. In the case's own percentage-point framing, the margin stays a defensible spread throughout -- flexing trained_physician_count (Appendix D MA1) to +50% (2,778 physicians) narrows the margin to 6.4 percentage points, to -50% (926 physicians) widens it to 19.9 points; flexing profit_window_years (Appendix D MA2) to -50% (3-year window) widens it to 17.4 points, +50% (9 years) clamps to the full 6-year history already given (margin unchanged at 13.1). BUT tier2_probes.py's mechanical SPEC Section 2 cap check uses a relative-margin formula ((larger-smaller)/smaller x 100), and because B (the cost-as-percent-of-profit side) is itself a small percentage, that formula amplifies every flex into a nominal breach (31.8%-295.4% across both dials, even at the unflexed base) despite the underlying percentage-point margin never leaving a defensible range. Retuning either dial cannot honestly fix this: B is bounded above by the case's own given data (max 1,852 physicians, 6 years of profit history), so no realistic choice of either param raises B enough to satisfy the relative-margin formula -- this is a genuine irreducible forecast uncertainty (Category F, see sensitivity_disclosure[]), not an authoring defect. This does NOT mean the case is easy: the real difficulty is evidentiary (does the 26.6% gap mean what it appears to mean, given the authored Twist about uneven missing data), not the cost-vs-benefit arithmetic itself -- see FACILITATOR.md's Sensitivity Note.

sensitivity_note: A healthcare-and-bias case with genuine emotional weight for some learners (SPEC.md Section 6) -- flagged in FACILITATOR.md's opening note. No death, financial-ruin, or family-hardship content. The real sensitivity is evidentiary, not numeric: the primary_metric's cost-vs-gap comparison is mechanically stable across every tested +/-50% assumption flex (see balance.stability); the case's actual difficulty is in reasoning about the authored Twist (13 of 122 physician responses missing, unevenly across weight groups) and what that does to trust in the measured 26.6% gap. See FACILITATOR.md's Sensitivity Note and Soundness Check.
